query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The unexpectedly low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its solution-treated, single–fcc–phase state arise because (i) Ti is forced into a random f.c.c. solid solution that possesses a comparatively HIGH intrinsic stacking-fault energy (SFE) and very little short-range chemical order (SRO), and (ii) the high SFE enables easy cross-slip and rapid dynamic recovery, preventing the build-up of dislocation forests. Low dislocation storage gives a small work-hardening rate, yielding a soft, readily plastic, and machinable alloy. If SFE is reduced and SRO/incipient Ti-rich ordering is introduced (e.g. by a low-temperature ageing treatment that allows local rearrangement or nano-precipitation without forming coarse intermetallics), cross-slip will be impeded, dislocations will tangle, and hardness/yield strength will rise while ductility falls.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy, homogenised 1150 °C/2 h + water quench → single-phase f.c.c. grains ~20–50 µm, no detectable secondary phases, random solid solution.
generation.intervention: Sub-solvus isothermal ageing at 650–750 °C for 2 h to promote chemical short-range ordering / incipient B2 or L1₀ nano-clusters and concomitant SFE reduction, without allowing coarse Laves/B2 precipitation.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static uniaxial tension (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹) or Vickers micro-hardness; grain structure kept unchanged (no recrystallisation) by using short ageing times; tests performed below 0.3 Tₘ to avoid dynamic strain ageing.
generation.structural_mediator: Magnitude of the intrinsic stacking-fault energy and the extent of Ti-driven short-range chemical ordering within the f.c.c. matrix.
generation.mechanism: 1. Solutionised state: random placement of large Ti atoms raises local lattice strain but electronically increases SFE; high SFE → easy cross-slip of partials → rapid dynamic recovery → low dislocation density → low work-hardening, hardness ~150–200 HV and σy ≈ 400–600 MPa with high uniform elongation. 2. Aged state: partial Ti clustering/SRO lowers SFE and creates short-range ordered obstacles; partial dislocations become less mobile, wide stacking faults narrow, dislocation interactions increase, forest hardening rises → hardness and yield strength increase (~+30–60 %), uniform elongation drops.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the solutionised baseline, aged samples will show: (a) SFE reduced by ≥20 %; (b) average stacking fault width reduced by ~30–50 %; (c) TEM reveals higher statistically stored dislocation density and fewer cross-slip events; (d) Vickers hardness and 0.2 % proof stress increase by at least 30 – 60 %; (e) uniform elongation decreases by ≥10 % absolute.
generation.baseline: Solutionised alloy: Vickers hardness 150–200 HV; 0.2 % yield strength 400–600 MPa; ultimate tensile strength 650–800 MPa; uniform elongation >40 %; wide stacking-fault ribbons (~5–8 nm) and low dislocation density after 10 % strain.
generation.boundary: Applies to CoCrFeNiTi compositions with 0.9 ≤ Ti/(Co+Cr+Fe+Ni+Ti) ≤ 1.1 kept as single-fcc solid solution; grain size 10–100 µm; tests at T ≤ 0.3 Tₘ (~400 °C). Hypothesis does not cover states containing >2 vol % coarse B2/Laves precipitates or heavily cold-worked or nano-grained conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Actual quantitative change in SFE with Ti ordering is inferred from alloy-chemistry trends but not yet measured; ageing may simultaneously cause minor precipitation that also contributes to strengthening, complicating separation of SRO vs precipitation effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples: (i) solutionised reference (1150 °C/2 h WQ); (ii) aged 650 °C/2 h; (iii) aged 750 °C/2 h. Confirm single f.c.c. phase + nanoscale ordering by synchrotron XRD and HRTEM/APT. Measure (a) SFE via weak-beam TEM or in-situ TEM fault-width analysis; (b) Vickers hardness; (c) tensile σy, UTS, uniform elongation; (d) post-deformation dislocation structures by TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If ageing does NOT simultaneously (1) reduce measured SFE and stacking-fault widths and (2) raise hardness/strength by at least 20 % while lowering ductility relative to the solutionised state, OR if solutionised specimens already show low SFE (<30 mJ m⁻²) with dense dislocation forests yet low hardness, the hypothesis is falsified.
